title: Standards, Trust and Parliamentary Safeguards
label: 4 November 2026 · Commissioner for Standards
summary: Daniel Greenberg, the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards, told the committee that ethical standards in Parliament protect the UK’s unwritten constitution because they sustain public consent through trust. He distinguished immediate, confrontational threats from slow erosion of democratic norms, argued that codes of conduct are mainly tools for encouraging good behaviour (backed by enforcement when needed), and urged more openness, engagement and practical checks—especially better scrutiny of legislation and more direct routes for civil society to influence lawmaking.

glossary.definition: Seven standards for public life (selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership).
Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority, which oversees MPs' expenses and pay.
A form of secondary legislation used to make or change law without a new Act of Parliament.
A parliamentary committee that examines secondary legislation for legal and drafting issues.

chapters.title: Why standards matter
chapters.takeaway: Standards matter because public consent to be governed rests on trust in institutions and people.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is maintaining high ethical standards among public figures important for protecting our constitutional democracy?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: Yes. I framed it by asking what the constitution needs protecting from. There are overt threats, like unrest, and slower threats where democratic norms erode.

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: Our unwritten constitution is a liberal democracy that governs by consent. Consent rests on trust: people must trust institutions and those who run them.

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: Standards officials matter at points where trust risks being damaged. Scandals can be useful if the system shows how it fixes them—openness and remedy restore trust.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So standards and your role help keep people trusting the institution and so protect consent?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: Exactly. If people see parliamentarians holding themselves to high standards, public trust is strengthened and consent maintained.

chapters.title: Codes, encouragement and enforcement
chapters.takeaway: Codes are vital for encouraging good conduct; enforcement is necessary but must be balanced with self-regulation.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: We have many codes, yet failures still occur. Do codes of conduct help encourage and enforce good behaviour?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: We should separate encouragement from enforcement. Codes are great for setting expectations and supporting good practice.

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: I publish advice notes and do outreach to help MPs meet standards. Much of my work is about helping people put things right, not just punishing them.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: But codes without accountability worry me. Should we build more accountability into the system?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: There must be teeth. The code I enforce can lead to public sanctions. But whether to add statutory backing is a question for Parliament, not for me.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: Would statutory rules give more authority?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: They give different authority. Statute can elevate or outsource authority; self-regulation is constitutionally significant here, so we should weigh trade-offs.

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: The code uses the Nolan principles. Some rules must be precise—like registration of gifts—while principles cover honesty and integrity, which are judged case by case.

chapters.title: Parliament’s role as a constitutional safeguard
chapters.takeaway: Parliament can safeguard the constitution but faces challenges from faster policymaking, weaker scrutiny and more secondary law.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: Would you consider the parliamentary standards system a constitutional safeguard?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: Yes. Because standards officials can improve trust and demonstrate self-correction, which supports the constitutional order.

turns.speaker: Lord Cryer
turns.text: Do you think Parliament acts as a safeguard when a government with a big majority wants to act unconstitutionally?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: Parliament can act as a safeguard, but scrutiny has weakened in places. I’ve written about limits to line-by-line scrutiny and urged more effective checks.

turns.speaker: Lord Cryer
turns.text: House of Commons scrutiny has declined: timetabling, fewer backbench amendment opportunities, and much more secondary legislation.

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: Exactly. And there’s an additional danger: replacing law with guidance or quasi-legislation lets ministers exercise power without proper parliamentary scrutiny.

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: Committees like the Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments are influential, but they lack formal powers. Parliament should consider where to strengthen checks.

chapters.title: Practical steps to restore trust and engagement
chapters.takeaway: More openness, engagement with civil society, explanation of policy and practical scrutiny tools would strengthen trust.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You said engagement matters. Is there a lack of constitutional knowledge among parliamentarians, and how might we fix it?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: It’s not that individuals lack knowledge so much as the institution sometimes lacks the time and processes to use expertise in policy-making.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: Would professional advisers on Public Bill committees, like Private Bill committees have, help line-by-line scrutiny?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: That’s a promising practical idea worth considering; Members are ready to engage if you give them the right brief and support.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: Any other practical engagement ideas for reducing vulnerabilities?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: One proposal: allow third-sector organisations to table amendments (they wouldn’t move them) so their concerns appear directly in parliamentary papers.

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: More broadly: publish clearer advice, explain policy choices better, and create direct routes for civil society to feed into the process.

turns.speaker: Lord Waldegrave of North Hill
turns.text: Some argue lack of trust comes from policy delivery failure—not small scandals. If living standards stagnate, trust falls even with honest politicians.

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: That’s partly about explanation and listening. Even when outcomes disappoint, better explanation of trade-offs and real listening can sustain consent.

chapters.title: Limits, values and concluding points
chapters.takeaway: Self-regulation, openness and practical reforms can protect the constitution, but Parliament must choose the balance of accountability and statute.

turns.speaker: Lord Griffiths of Burry Port
turns.text: You’ve combined encouragement with calling out bad behaviour. Is your approach comparable to community or religious discipline?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: My role is value-neutral and institutional. I use the Nolan principles as a practical ethical framework that works beyond religious language.

turns.speaker: Lord Griffiths of Burry Port
turns.text: But you do sometimes need to call people out?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: Yes. Encouragement must be backed by accountability when support fails; my office balances outreach with public investigations and sanctions.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: Do we currently have enough accountability?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: I won’t prescribe the answer. Self-regulation is constitutionally important; deciding whether to add statutory measures is for Parliament to weigh carefully.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final thoughts?

turns.speaker: Daniel Greenberg
turns.text: Standards officials can help preserve trust by being independent, open, corrective and helpful. Practical changes—better scrutiny, engagement and explanation—would strengthen constitutional safeguards.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. That concludes our session.
